stops.name: Pescara, the birth house on Corso Manthonè
stops.campa: In the house of Francesco Paolo Rapagnetta-d'Annunzio, above the fish-smelling river port of Pescara, a son is born on 12 March 1863. The Adriatic light comes in off the water and fills the room. The father, half-drunk on pride, will spend a fortune making a prince of him. The midwives say the child does not cry. The name itself is an annunciation: d'Annunzio, of the Announcement; the family hears the angel in it, and so will Italy.

stops.name: The Adriatic off Pescara, the legend of the brigantine Irene
stops.campa: The other birth, the one the poet himself will tell: not in a bed but on the deck of the brigantine Irene, pitching in the March Adriatic, the newborn washed by spray before he is washed by any priest. Born on the sea, of the sea: the legend runs ahead of the man all his life, and he never contradicts it, because it is truer than the register of the parish. The wave that rocked the cradle will carry him to Buccari and to Fiume.

stops.name: Prato, the Cicognini college
stops.campa: Eleven years old, the boy is sent north to the Cicognini at Prato, the sternest college in Tuscany, so that the Abruzzo dialect may be burned out of him and pure Tuscan set in its place. He writes home that he intends to be first in everything, and he is: first in Latin, first in insubordination, first in the punishment cells. In the dormitory he reads Carducci by contraband candle. The masters record a prodigy; the prodigy records himself.

stops.name: Chieti, Primo Vere printed at sixteen
stops.campa: Still a schoolboy in uniform, he gives the printer Ricci of Chieti a sheaf of verses in the metres of Carducci's Odi barbare. His father pays for the edition. Primo Vere, First Spring, goes out into Italy signed by a sixteen-year-old, and Giuseppe Chiarini reviews it in the Fanfulla della Domenica: a new poet exists. In the college at Prato the boy reads his own name in the national press and understands, once and for all, that fame is a substance that can be manufactured.

stops.name: The road to Francavilla, the first death of the poet
stops.campa: On 13 November 1880 the Gazzetta della Domenica of Florence announces that Gabriele d'Annunzio, the young poet of whom it has often spoken, has died on the road to Francavilla, thrown from his horse. Italy mourns the boy Muse. The letter announcing the death was written by the poet himself, signed G. Rutini; days later he rises from the dead to publish the corrected second edition of Primo Vere. It is the first myth he authors of himself: he learns that his own death is his best material, and he will die twice more before the end.

stops.name: Prato, the licence with honour, the college left behind
stops.campa: In the summer of 1881 he takes his licenza with honour and walks out of the Cicognini gates for the last time, eighteen years old, already the author of two books and one resurrection. Elda Zucconi, his Tuscan first love, is left behind in the pages of Canto Novo taking the sea-name Lalla. The masters who caned him will boast of him for a century. He turns south for one last Abruzzo summer, then aims himself at Rome like a projectile.

stops.name: Rome, arrival at Termini, the university abandoned before it begins
stops.campa: In November 1881 the train from the Abruzzo sets him down in Umbertine Rome. He enrols in Letters at the Sapienza and never sits an examination: the city itself is the faculty. Byzantine Rome of the speculators and the salons takes the small, cat-eyed provincial and finds him already fluent in its language. Within weeks he is in the newspapers; within a year he is the most talked-of young man in the capital. The Tiber, he decides, is his second river after the Pescara.

stops.name: Via dell'Umiltà, Cronaca Bizantina and Canto Novo
stops.campa: Angelo Sommaruga's Cronaca Bizantina gathers the golden youth of literary Rome, and d'Annunzio becomes its ornament. In May 1882 Sommaruga publishes Canto Novo, verses salted with the Adriatic, sunburnt, pagan: Rome discovers that the boy poet has a body and is not ashamed of it. He writes society chronicle, he duels in print, he dresses beyond his means. The Bizantina crowd calls itself decadent as a boast; he alone means to make decadence into empire.
stops.quote: Bisogna fare la propria vita, come si fa un'opera d'arte.
stops.quote_source: Il Piacere (1889), the credo already lived in the Roman years

stops.name: Florence, the elopement train with Maria Hardouin
stops.campa: At the end of June 1883 he boards the Florence train with Maria Hardouin di Gallese, the duke's daughter, twenty years old and already carrying his child. The scandal is arranged like a stanza: flight, pursuit, discovery in Florence, the ruined honour of a ducal house. Rome talks of nothing else, which is the point. The duke rages, the mother relents, and the poet, who has read every romance and written better ones, waits calmly for the wedding he has made inevitable.

stops.name: Rome, the marriage in the chapel of Palazzo Altemps
stops.campa: On 28 July 1883, in the private chapel of Palazzo Altemps, Gabriele d'Annunzio marries Maria Hardouin di Gallese. The duke does not attend. The groom is twenty, famous, and insolvent; the bride's family considers itself dishonoured by a poet and does not yet know that in fifty years the poet will be the only reason it is remembered. Mario, the first of three sons, is born in January. The marriage will dissolve into affairs and debts, but the title of duchess consort trails him like incense.

stops.name: La Tribuna, Duca Minimo, chronicler of elegance
stops.campa: For the Tribuna he becomes Duca Minimo, the Smallest Duke, and invents modern celebrity journalism from inside: chronicles of concerts, funerals, jewellers' windows, women's shoulders at the Palazzo Farnese balls. He furnishes the Roman bourgeoisie with its dreams and prices. From these columns he quarries Il Piacere; every countess he describes is a study, every drawing-room a set. He earns much, spends triple, and learns the arithmetic of glamour: debt is merely fame that has not yet been paid for.

stops.name: Outside Porta del Popolo, the saber duel and the scar
stops.campa: Journalism in Byzantine Rome is settled with sabers. In the meadows beyond the walls the poet meets the journalist Carlo Magnico on the field of honour and takes a blade across the scalp. The wound is dressed with iron perchloride; the tradition holds that the treatment costs him his hair, and the famous gleaming skull of the Comandante is minted here, on a Roman duelling ground, at twenty-two. He fights other duels and loses none of them in the telling. The scar becomes part of the iconography.
